title: Hello World
subtitle: Words by the Fire
martuIntro:
Hi. It is me, Mar'tu. Before we continue on our adventure, we go back to the first words, yes?
A lot of that campaign code felt like a wall, yes? We will take the wall apart, one stone at a time.
Every spell begins as words. Python is fussy about words. More fussy than Lucky is about glug, yes?
Tonight: how to say something, how to keep something in a box, and how to let Python do the math.
goals: Make Python show words on the screen
Keep words or a number in a named box (a variable)
Change what is in a box
Let Python do the math with your boxes
Join words and numbers into one line, and draw a mana bar from blocks
Read Python's error messages and fix small mistakes

items.title: How Mar'tu Teaches
items.summary: One minute: how ▶ Run, 💡 Help and Your steps work.
items.body:
Press ▶ [[run|Run]], above your code. Python answers in the [[console|Console]], under your code.
Running unfinished code is fine. An error is not a grade: it says what Python couldn't read.
Your steps: ✓ done, ● the step you're on, ○ still to come.
Stuck? Press 💡 Help, under the Console. Each press gives more, up to the line itself. Your hints are private.
Nothing here is timed.

exercises.title: What an error looks like
exercises.martu: `print` means show on the screen, not on paper: this line shows `Shield up.` in the [[console|Console]], the box under your code. Press ▶ Run, just above your code. Then you'll break it on purpose, and Python will show an [[error message]]. That's not a grade. It's like a teacher's note in the margin: it points to the spot.

anotherWay.text:
Press *Show Python's full message* in the box, and you see this:
```text
File "main.py", line 1
  print("Shield up.)
        ^
SyntaxError: unterminated ...
```
1. Read the last line first. *Syntax* is how a line is put together, as in English class, so a *SyntaxError* is a line Python can't read.
2. *Unterminated* means never ended: the text has no closing quote.
3. The top line gives the line number, line 1. Fix that line.

anotherWay.label: Something everyday
anotherWay.text: It is like a friend saying "I couldn't read the end of your note." They are not upset. They are telling you where to look.

exercises.title: Where the symbols live
exercises.martu:
`-` is minus, as in math. `_` is the underscore (Shift and `-`): it stands in for a space, as in `max_mana`. `=` is the equals key, but in Python it won't mean equals. More in Boxes With Labels. Top right of your keyboard:
```text
with Shift:   (   )   _   +
no Shift:     9   0   -   =
```
`print` means show on the screen, not on paper. `#` is Shift+3.

anotherWay.text:
The three keys, circled:
```text
  9   0  (-)  (=)   Backspace
         Shift + (-) gives (_)
```

1. `-` is the key right after `0`.
2. `_` is the same key with Shift held down.
3. `=` is the next key to the right.
4. `"` is Shift with the `'` key, next to Enter.
5. `#` is Shift with the `3` key.

anotherWay.label: Say it shorter
anotherWay.text: Type `print("`, then the three symbols, then `")`.

Quotes mean *show these exact marks*. Python shows whatever is between them, as it is: `print("( )")` shows `( )`.
Type `print("_ - = are side by side.")` on line 2. Anything inside the quotes shows as it is.

exercises.title: Quotes and parentheses come in pairs
exercises.martu: [[quotes|Quotes]] come in pairs, like quotation marks in English class. [[parentheses|Parentheses]] `( )` come in pairs too, as in math: 3 × (2 + 4). Line 1 needs a closing quote, and line 2 needs a `)`. To [[mend]] a line means to fix it, and a *slip* is a small mistake. Press Run, read the box, and mend one line at a time.

anotherWay.text:
Quotes are bookends. Words stand between them:
```text
print("It is not a compass")
     ^^                   ^^
   ( and "           " and )
    open               close
```
The `(` opens first and the `)` closes last, around the quotes, like (2 + 4) in math.

anotherWay.label: Something everyday
anotherWay.text: Shoes come in pairs. One shoe is not a pair. One quote mark is not a pair either.

1. Python finds the first quote and starts reading words.
2. It looks for the next quote, to know where the words stop.
3. It never comes. Python reaches the end of the line and stops: *unterminated*, which means never ended.

anotherWay.label: Say it shorter
anotherWay.text: Line 1 needs a `"`. Line 2 needs a `)`.

exercises.title: Words need quotes
exercises.martu: Text you want to show needs [[quotes]], like someone's exact words in English class. Without quotes, Python thinks the word is a name it should already know, and looks it up. (You'll make names like that in Boxes With Labels.) Here it finds nothing, so it stops and says *not defined*.

anotherWay.text:
What Python tries with `print(Fireball)`:
1. No quotes, so this is not text to show.
2. Then it must be a name Python should already know.
3. Python looks for the name `Fireball`. Nothing has that name yet.
4. It stops and says *not defined*.

anotherWay.label: From English class
anotherWay.text: In English, quotes can show you mean the word itself: *'Lucky' has five letters.* Without quotes, *Lucky* means the hero. Python works the same way: quotes mean the word itself.

anotherWay.label: This, not this
anotherWay.text:
Not this: `print(Fireball)`. Python looks for a name and finds nothing.
This: `print("Fireball")`. Python shows the word.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? Names versus words
anotherWay.text: Python has two kinds of words. Words in quotes are shown exactly. Words without quotes are names: Python looks them up. `print` itself is a name with no quotes, and Python finds it. `Fireball` is a name with no quotes too, and Python finds nothing.

anotherWay.text: Show words? Use quotes.

items.title: Boxes With Labels
items.summary: Keep words or a number in a named box, use the exact name, and change what is inside.

exercises.title: A box with a name
exercises.martu:
In math, a letter like x stands for a number. A box (a [[variable]]) is like that, but you pick its name, and it can hold words. In `companion = "Gearshift"`, the box's name is `companion`, like a label on the box. In math, `=` means both sides are equal. In Python, read `=` as *gets*: companion gets Gearshift.
```
  companion
+-----------+
| Gearshift |
+-----------+
```

anotherWay.text:
Two lines, two answers:
```
print(companion)
-> looks inside the box
-> shows Gearshift

print("companion")
-> these exact letters
-> shows companion
```

anotherWay.label: Like a phone contact
anotherWay.text: A phone contact has a name with a number saved under it. Tap the name, and the phone uses what is saved. `print(companion)` taps the name. `print("companion")` only reads the word out loud.

anotherWay.label: In Tor
anotherWay.text: A jar on my shelf with a name chalked on it: `companion`. Inside is Gearshift. Ask for the jar by its name, and you get what is inside.

Python reads one line at a time:
1. `companion = "Gearshift"`: the box `companion` gets Gearshift.
2. `print(companion)`: looks inside the box and shows Gearshift.
3. `print("companion")`: shows the letters companion.

anotherWay.label: Not this
anotherWay.text:
Not this: `"companion" = "Gearshift"` (a box's name never goes in quotes). Not this: `companion - "Gearshift"` (`-` means minus). Not this: `"Gearshift"` on its own (no name in front, so Python reads it and throws it away).
This: `companion = "Gearshift"`.

exercises.title: Numbers don't get quotes
exercises.martu: A [[number]] gets no quotes. `3` is an amount you can do math with, like points in a game. `"3"` in quotes is text, like the 3 on a jersey: nobody adds two jerseys. In the Example, `26` has no quotes, so `max_mana` holds a number. Lucky's armor bonus is 3.

anotherWay.text:
Two boxes that look alike:
```
armor_bonus = 3
^ a number: Python can
  do math with it

armor_bonus = "3"
^ text: the mark 3,
  like a word
```

anotherWay.label: A jersey number
anotherWay.text: The 3 on a jersey names a player. Nobody adds two jerseys, so that 3 is like text. Points in a game are an amount you add up, so they are a number. Ask: would I ever do math with this?
Python looks at the value. It sees `3` and makes a number. It sees `"3"` and makes text, because quotes always mean text.

anotherWay.label: Why "3" isn't 3
anotherWay.text: Quotes mean these exact letters. `"3"` is the mark 3, the way `"glug"` is the letters g-l-u-g. Python won't do math with text. Next lesson you will add numbers, so keep them free of quotes.
Words get quotes. Numbers don't.

A box holds one value at a time, like a small whiteboard: write 26, wipe it, write 21. In math, x = 26 and x = 21 can't both be true. In Python they happen one after the other, top to bottom, and only the newest value stays.
Guess what prints, then press Run.

exercises.martu:
Python does math with [[math signs]]: `+` (plus), `-` (minus), `*` (times: there's no × key) and `/` (divided by). `print(9 * 2)` shows 18.
A gap is the hours between two leyline bursts. On my chalk wall, the first gap was 48, the last 37.
In math, area = length × width works for any rectangle. Make your line a formula too: I test it with other numbers.

```text
[ first_gap: 48 ]

[ last_gap: 37 ]
```

exercises.title: Let Python do the math
exercises.martu:
Don't work the total out yourself. Write the math with the box names and let Python work it out, like a formula. In math class, this is [[show your work]]. The Example does it: `map_cost = map_count * map_price`.
Python is not a spreadsheet: when a number changes, press Run again, and the total changes to match.

anotherWay.label: Arrows into the total
anotherWay.text:
```text
lantern_count * lantern_price
  --> lantern_cost

rope_count * rope_price
  --> rope_cost

lantern_cost + rope_cost
  --> total_cost
```
Change any box on the left and press Run again: the arrows carry the new number all the way to the total.

anotherWay.label: An online cart
anotherWay.text: In an online cart, you change the quantity from 3 to 7 and press Update. The cart works out the total again from quantity × price. It never keeps a typed-in total. In Python, Run is your Update button.

anotherWay.label: Show your work
anotherWay.text: In math class, a teacher wants your work, not only the answer. Python is the same. `total_cost = 22` is only the answer. `total_cost = lantern_cost + rope_cost` is the work, and Python does it again every time you press Run.
Cost = how many `*` price of one. Total = cost `+` cost. Never type the answer.

exercises.title: Spend some mana
exercises.martu:
In math class, x = x − 3 has no answer. But Python's `=` isn't a math statement. Python works out the right side first, with what's in the box now: 26 − 3 is 23. Then 23 goes back in the box: `mana = mana - spell_cost`.
Read it as: mana gets mana minus spell cost. To cast a spell means to use it once.

```text
  -> put it back
```

5. `print(mana)` shows 17.

exercises.title: Glue words together
exercises.martu:
`+` has two jobs. Between numbers it adds: `2 + 3` is 5. Between texts it [[glue|glues]], like a compound word: `"sun" + "flower"` is `"sunflower"`, with no space. To glue a number, make it text first with [[str()|`str()`]], short for *string*: `str(26)` gives `"26"`.
`"Mana: " + 26` makes Python stop. `"Mana: " + str(26)` works. Spaces are text too, so put them inside the quotes.

```text
[Lucky] + [ has ] + [26] + [ mana.]

```

exercises.title: A status line
exercises.martu:
A status line shows a hero's name and mana, like the stats text in a game: `Oogrish: 18/18 mana`. Max mana is the most mana a hero can hold. It is twice the magical affinity, how strong the hero's magic is. Twice means times 2.
The 0s on lines 3 and 4 are placeholders: their `#` notes say what goes there. Any hero can go in `hero_name`.

anotherWay.label: A status bar
anotherWay.text:
```text
Oogrish  :   18   /   18   mana
```

exercises.title: Repeat a mark
exercises.martu:
In math, 3 × 4 means 4 + 4 + 4. Python can [[stamp]] text the same way: `"█" * 3` means `"█" + "█" + "█"`, so it shows `███`.
A mana bar is full blocks `█` for the mana you have, then empty blocks `░` for the mana used. `+` glues the two parts. `*` repeats one text a number of times.

anotherWay.label: A fuel gauge
anotherWay.text:
```text
mana 3 of 5:   [ █ █ █ ░ ░ ]
                 have   used
                 3      5 - 3
```

anotherWay.label: A stamp
anotherWay.text: A rubber stamp makes the same mark again and again. `full * mana` presses the full stamp mana times. `empty * (max_mana - mana)` presses the empty stamp once for each point used.

anotherWay.label: What Python does first
anotherWay.text:
For `empty * (max_mana - mana)` with mana 3 of 5:
1. PEMDAS, parentheses first: `5 - 3` is 2.
2. Then `empty * 2` stamps `░░`.
Without parentheses, Python does `empty * 5` first, then `"░░░░░" - 3`, and text minus a number is an error.

anotherWay.label: Why parentheses?
anotherWay.text: Python does `*` before `-`, the same as PEMDAS in math class. Parentheses say: do this part first.
Full: `full * mana`. Empty: `empty * (max_mana - mana)`. Glue them with `+`.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: `get_mana_bar` had `filled = "█" * caster["mana"]` and `empty = "░" * (caster["max_mana"] - caster["mana"])`. Your line is the same bar.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: A mana bar is a tape diagram. The full part and the empty part make the whole: 3 have + 2 used = 5 max. So the empty part is the whole minus the full part, `max_mana - mana`.

This spell has four [[bug|bugs]]: mistakes in code. Two are loud: they make Python stop with an error. Fix those first, one at a time. Two are quiet: Python runs, and `Rope: 10 coins` looks right, but for the wrong reason.

anotherWay.text:
1. Press Run. Python stops at the first loud bug. Read the box: its title, then Python's last line. Fix the line it gives.
2. Press Run again, and fix the next one.
3. When Python no longer stops, read the message under each step.

anotherWay.label: Two kinds of bug
anotherWay.text:
```text
loud bugs:
Python stops, and its
message gives the line.

quiet bugs:
the program runs, but
the answer is wrong.
```

`hours_waited += 6` is a short way to write `hours_waited = hours_waited + 6`. Read it as *hours waited goes up by 6*. `mana -= 3` means `mana = mana - 3`: mana goes down by 3.

items.title: Chalk Quiz
items.summary: Eight questions on quotes, boxes, math and glue. Retake as often as you like.

questions.q: Which line makes a box named `hero` that holds the text Lucky?

whyWrong.0: `def` is for something you'll learn in Unit 3. To make a box, write the name, `=`, then the value.
whyWrong.1: A box's name never goes in quotes. In quotes, `"hero"` is only the letters h-e-r-o.
whyWrong.3: `-` is minus. To make a box, use `=`.

questions.explain: A box is `name = value`: the name with no quotes, `=`, then the text in quotes. Hero gets Lucky.

questions.q: What will this code show in the Console?
questions.explain: Each line works out the right side with what is in the box now: 18, then 13, then 8. The box keeps only its newest value.

questions.q: This line should show It is not a compass. Fix it.
questions.explain: Quotes come in pairs, like quotation marks in English class. Add the closing `"` before the `)`.

questions.q: What will this line show in the Console?
questions.explain: `*` repeats each text: two full blocks, then three empty blocks, glued together with `+`.

questions.q: Fill the blank so this line shows `Mana: 7`.
questions.explain: `str(7)` turns the number into text, so it can be glued to `"Mana: "`. `str` is short for string.

questions.q: Mar'tu had 3 lanterns, and the total was 22. Now he changes `lantern_count` to 5 and presses Run again. Which `total` line still gives the right answer, with nobody retyping it?

whyWrong.0: 22 is a typed-in answer for 3 lanterns. It stays 22 when the count changes.
whyWrong.1: 12 is the old lantern cost, typed in. It doesn't change to match the new count.
whyWrong.3: 3 is the old count, typed in. Use the box `lantern_count`.

questions.explain: Only the line with the box names changes to match when a box changes and the code runs again. It's a formula, not a typed-in answer.

whyWrong.0: The box is named `Health`, with a capital H. `health` is a different name.

items.title: The Night Watch Ledger
items.summary: Mar'tu's ledger, his notebook of costs, for the long night: mana for the barrier, oil for the lanterns, and who keeps watch.
items.intro:
A ledger is a notebook where you write down what things cost. Mar'tu keeps one for tonight. The barrier must hold until the next burst (a blast from the leylines), 37 hours away.
Three parts, in order: A. what we know, B. let the code combine it (do the math with the box names), C. write the ledger.
The barrier eats 2 mana an hour. The lanterns burn 1 flask (a small bottle) of oil an hour, and a flask costs 3 coins. *Per hour* is a unit rate, like miles per hour.
items.martu: Thirty-seven hours, yes? I don't want to do this math by hand in the middle of the night. Put what we know in boxes, let Python do the math with the box names, then write the ledger lines. If the clock changes its mind, change one box and press Run again: every line changes to match.

anotherWay.label: The ledger page
anotherWay.text:
```text
A. what we know
   37 hours, 2 mana/hour,
   1 flask/hour, 3 coins/flask
B. let the code combine it
   mana_needed, oil_needed,
   oil_cost
C. the ledger
   three printed lines
```
Each part only uses boxes from the parts above it.

1. Fill the four boxes in A.
2. In B, multiply: hours times per hour; flasks times price.
3. In C, glue words and `str()` of each box.
4. Press Run after every line.

anotherWay.label: Why a ledger?
anotherWay.text: The chalk wall says the next burst may come sooner: 32 hours, maybe. If you typed the answers, every line of the ledger would be wrong. With box names, you change one box and press Run again.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: In the campaign, the bursts came closer: 48, then 37, then about 32 hours. Here, my checks try 32 hours to see if your ledger changes to match.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: *Per hour* is a unit rate, like miles per hour. 37 hours at 2 mana per hour is 37 × 2 = 74 mana, the same way 3 hours at 60 miles per hour is 180 miles.

items.title: The Ward Sign
items.summary: Draw the word TOR in big block letters, one letter under another. Every mark comes from one box, `ink`, so one change to `ink` changes the whole sign.
items.intro:
Mar'tu wants a ward sign on the barrier post: a sign that helps protect the barrier. It spells `TOR` in big block letters, one letter under another, because the post is tall and thin.
Wards work better when they are tidy. Probably.
items.martu:
Each `print` draws one row of a letter. `ink * 5` stamps the mark in `ink` 5 times: `█████`. `"  " + ink` glues 2 spaces in front of one mark. Each letter is 5 rows tall.
Every row uses the box `ink`, so one change to `ink` changes the whole sign. I drew the T. You draw the rest, yes?

anotherWay.label: Graph paper
anotherWay.text:
Draw the letter on graph paper first. Each row of squares is one `print`. A filled square is `ink`. An empty square is a space inside quotes.
```
█████   print(ink * 5)
█   █   print(ink + "   " + ink)
```

items.title: Clock Math
items.summary: Three more math signs, `**`, `//` and `%`, and PEMDAS in Python. Then you work out where the Ley Clock's hand stops.
items.body:
Three more math signs. You don't need them for the campaign. They are here for the curious, yes?
1. `**` is a [[power]], like 2³ in math class: `2 ** 3` means 2 × 2 × 2, which is 8.
2. `//` is [[floor division]]. *Floor* means round down: divide, then keep only the whole part. In math class, 50 ÷ 12 = 4 R 2, and `50 // 12` gives the 4.
3. `%` gives the [[remainder]], what is left over: `50 % 12` gives the 2. Here `%` is not percent.
Python uses the [[order of operations]] you know from math class as PEMDAS. Parentheses first. Then `**`. Then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%`. Then `+` and `-`. So `2 + 3 * 4` is 14, but `(2 + 3) * 4` is 20.
Now the Ley Clock. It has 12 marks, numbered 0 to 11. After mark 11 comes mark 0 again, the way a wall clock goes from 12 back to 1. The hand moves one mark each hour.
The hand is on mark 9. Where is it 50 hours from now? Add first, then wrap: `(9 + 50) % 12` is 11.
The parentheses matter. `9 + 7 % 12` does the `%` first and gives 16, which is not even a mark. `(9 + 7) % 12` gives 4.
It is not a compass, Lucky. It is a clock. It goes around.

exercises.title: Where is the hand?
exercises.martu:
`%` gives the remainder. In math class, 50 ÷ 12 = 4 R 2, and `50 % 12` gives the 2. The Ley Clock has 12 marks, 0 to 11, so `% 12` wraps any count back onto the clock. Here `%` is not percent.
`50 // 12` gives the 4, the whole part. PEMDAS still works: add inside parentheses first, then wrap.

anotherWay.text:
The marks go around, then start again:
```
... 9 10 11 0 1 2 3 ...
```
Count 4 steps from 9: 10, 11, 0, 1. The hand stops on mark 1.

anotherWay.label: A wall clock
anotherWay.text: A wall clock does this. Three hours after 11 o'clock is 2 o'clock, not 14 o'clock. `(11 + 3) % 12` is 2.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: This is long division with a remainder. 50 ÷ 12 = 4 R 2: 12 fits into 50 four whole times, and 2 is left over. `50 // 12` gives the 4, and `50 % 12` gives the 2.

1. Add: `start + hours`.
2. Too big for the clock? Take away 12, and again, until it fits.
3. What is left is the mark. `% 12` does steps 2 and 3 at once.
`hand = (start + hours) % 12`. Parentheses first, then wrap.

items.title: Asking the Traveler: input()
items.summary: Let your program ask a question. The answer is always text, so `int()` turns it into a number.
items.body:
Sometimes a program should ask. The [[input]] command, `input()`, shows a question, called the [[prompt]], and waits for an answer.
Whatever comes back is text, like writing on a paper form. Even `3` comes back as the text `"3"`.
Text can't do math: `"3" + "3"` glues to `33`. To get a real number, use [[int]]: `int(input("Sips? "))`. `int` is short for integer, a whole number.
On this site, the answers come from the area labeled Input for your program, under your code, one answer per line. Change them and press Run again, as often as you like.
You've seen this before. In the campaign, `user.clicked()` handed back text, like `"option 1"`. That is why the dialogue code compared it with words in quotes.

examples.output:
Who knocks? Gearshift
Come in, Gearshift.

exercises.title: Who goes there?
exercises.martu:
`input()` asks a question and waits for the answer. The answer always comes back as text, like writing on a paper form. For math, wrap it in `int()`. `int` is short for integer, a whole number: `int("3")` gives 3.
The answers come from the area labeled Input for your program, under your code, one answer per line.

Come in, Lucky.

anotherWay.text:

```
typed 3
-> input() gives "3" (text)
-> int() gives 3 (a number)
-> 3 * 2 is 6
```

`input()` gives text. `int(input())` gives a number.

items.title: Quick Check 1 · Form A questions
items.summary: Three questions to check yourself. They don't decide whether you test out.

questions.q: What does this line show in the Console?

whyWrong.1: Look at `"] "`: there is a space after the `]`, and spaces are text too.
whyWrong.2: `*` stamps the block 3 times. It does not glue the number on.

questions.explain: `*` stamps: 3 full blocks, 2 empty ones. `"] "` adds the `]` and a space. `str()` turns 3 and 5 into text, so `+` can glue them.
In math, x = x − 2 has no answer, but in Python `=` means gets. Line 2 works out 5 − 2 with what is in `x` now, then puts 3 back in `x`. A box keeps only its latest value.

questions.q: Which line makes a box whose name Python accepts?

whyWrong.0: A name can't have a space. Python reads two names and stops. Use `_` instead.
whyWrong.2: A box's name never has quotes. Quotes make it text, and text can't be a name.

questions.explain: Names have no spaces and no quotes: `magical_affinity = 9`.

exercises.takeaway: Quotes come in pairs, numbers get no quotes, and names match letter for letter.

items.title: Quick Check 1 · Form B questions
items.summary: Three questions to check yourself. They don't decide whether you test out.

questions.q: What does this line show in the Console?

whyWrong.1: Look at `"] "`: there is a space after the `]`, and spaces are text too.
whyWrong.2: `*` stamps the block 2 times. It does not glue the number on.

questions.explain: `*` stamps: 2 full blocks, 4 empty ones. `"] "` adds the `]` and a space. `str()` turns 2 and 6 into text, so `+` can glue them.
In math, y = y − 3 has no answer, but in Python `=` means gets. Line 2 works out 8 − 3 with what is in `y` now, then puts 5 back in `y`. A box keeps only its latest value.

questions.q: Which line makes a box whose name Python accepts?

whyWrong.0: A name can't have a space. Python reads two names and stops. Use `_` instead.
whyWrong.2: A box's name never has quotes. Quotes make it text, and text can't be a name.

questions.explain: Names have no spaces and no quotes: `spell_color = "teal"`. The value can have quotes. The name can't.

items.title: Mar'tu's Chalk Notes: First Words
items.summary: Everything from Unit 1 on one page. Printable.

entries.note: `print` shows text on the screen, in the Console. Quotes and parentheses come in pairs: one opens, one closes. (Lesson: Words in Quotes)
`print()` with nothing inside prints an empty line.
A line that starts with `#` is a note for people (a comment), like a stage direction in a play. Python skips it, so a `#` in front of a line switches that line off.
Read `=` as gets: companion gets Gearshift. A box's name never has quotes. Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label. (Lesson: Boxes With Labels)
A number gets no quotes, so Python can do math with it. `"3"` in quotes is text, like the 3 on a jersey: nobody adds two jerseys.
Read it as: mana gets mana minus spell cost. In math, x = x − 3 has no answer, but Python works out the right side first, then puts the answer back in the box.
`*` means times (there's no × key) and `/` means divided by. `/` always gives a decimal, like `24.0`. (Lesson: Math and Glue)

entries.concept: How many × how much is one
entries.note: Put each number in a named box. Then write the math with the box names, like a formula in math class. Change a number and press Run again: the total changes to match. Never type the total in yourself.
`+` glues text to text, like a compound word: sun + flower is sunflower. A number must become text first, with `str()`, short for string (text). Spaces are text too.
`*` stamps one text a number of times, like repeated addition: `"█" * 3` is `"█" + "█" + "█"`.
PEMDAS, as in math class: Python does `*` before `-`, so put the subtraction in parentheses.
Python's last line: `SyntaxError: unterminated string literal`. Syntax means how a line is put together, like grammar. Some text in quotes never closes. Add the missing quote.
Python's last line: `SyntaxError: '(' was never closed`. A `(` has no `)` to match it. Add the missing `)`.

entries.concept: Error: a name it doesn't know
entries.note: Python's last line: `NameError: name 'max_mana' is not defined`. Python has no box with that exact name. Names match letter for letter, capitals too.

entries.concept: Error: a space in a name
entries.note: Python's last line: `SyntaxError: invalid syntax`. Python can't read the line, because a name can't have a space. Use `_` instead: `magical_affinity`.
Python's last line: `TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str`. Concatenate means glue, str means text and int means a whole number: you can only glue text to text. Use `str(7)`.
Python's last line starts with `SyntaxError`. `def` is for something you'll learn in Unit 3. To make a box, write the name, `=`, then the value: `character = "Zelda"`.

entries.output:
Glug canteen: half full.
Smell: still terrible.
entries.note: Three quote marks start text that can go over many lines, and three more end it. It is not a `#` note: Python prints it. (Extra practice: Many lines at once)
`mana -= 3` is short for `mana = mana - 3`. (Extra practice: The short way)
In 50 ÷ 12 = 4 R 2, `//` gives the 4 and `%` gives the 2. Here `%` is not percent. `**` is a power: `2 ** 3` is 8. (Article: Clock Math)
`input()` always hands back text. `int()` makes it a number: `int` is short for integer, a whole number. (Article: Asking the Traveler)
